statement.p: The following questions refer to the table shown below, giving the temperature adjusted for wind-chill, C, in {}^\circ F, as a function f(w,T) of the wind speed, w, in mph, and the temperature, T, in {}^\circ F. The temperature adjusted for wind-chill tells you how cold it feels, as a result of the combination of wind and temperature.

p.em: Be sure you can state in practical terms what your answer means.
Be sure you can state in practical terms what your answer means.

static.solution:
(a) For f_w(20, 20) we know f_w(w_0, t_0) \approx \frac{f(w_0 + h,t_0) - f(w_0,t_0)}{h}.
Thus, we have f_w(20, 20) \approx \frac{3 - 4}{5} = -0.2.
Note that we could also approximate the partial derivative by taking a difference quotient with the point to the left of 20 (that is, taking f_w(20,20)\approx \frac{f(20,20) - f(20-5),20}{5}, or by taking a central difference, f_w(20,20)\approx \frac{f(20+5,20) - f(20-5,20)}{10}.
This means that when the wind speed is 20 mph and the true temperature is 20 {}^\circ F, as the wind speed increases from 20 mph by 1 mph we feel an approximately -0.2^\circ F drop in temperature. This rate is negative because the temperature you feel drops as the wind speed increases.
(b) For f_t(15, 10) we know f_t(w_0, t_0) \approx \frac{f(w_0,t_0 + h) - f(w_0,t_0)}{h}.
Thus, we have f_t(15, 10) \approx \frac{(0 + 7)}{5} = 1.4.
Note that we could also approximate the partial derivative by taking a difference quotient with the point to the left of 10 (that is, taking f_t(15,10)\approx \frac{f(15,10) - f(15,10-5)}{5}, or by taking a central difference, f_t(15,10)\approx \frac{f(15,10+5) - f(15,10-5)}{10}.
This means that when the wind speed is 15 mph and the true temperature is 10 {}^\circ F, the apparent temperature increases by approximately 1.4^\circ F for an increase of 1^\circ F in the true temperature. This rate is positive because the temperature you feel increases as the true temperature increases.
